nodes.name: Vienna
nodes.tagline: Imperial capital, incubator of modernism
nodes.summary: For six centuries the seat of the Habsburgs, Vienna entered the twentieth century as a city where music, psychoanalysis, painting and logic were all being rebuilt at once. Its coffee houses put physicists, composers and philosophers at the same tables, which is why so many modern ideas carry a Viennese accent.

nodes.name: Gustav Mahler
nodes.tagline: Composer who stretched the symphony to its limit
nodes.summary: Mahler ran the Vienna Court Opera by day and wrote enormous symphonies in summer huts, treating the form as something that should contain the whole world. His harmonic restlessness handed the next generation the door out of tonality.

facts.label: Motto
facts.value: A symphony must be like the world

nodes.name: Sigmund Freud
nodes.tagline: Mapped the mind as something that hides from itself
nodes.summary: Working from a consulting room at Berggasse 19, Freud proposed that the greater part of mental life is unconscious and reachable only obliquely, through dreams, slips and free association. Whether or not the theory held, the vocabulary it produced is now inseparable from how people describe themselves.

nodes.name: Gustav Klimt
nodes.tagline: Gold leaf, ornament and unsettling eroticism
nodes.summary: Klimt broke from the academic establishment to lead the Vienna Secession, then spent his gold period fusing Byzantine mosaic surfaces with frankly sexual subject matter. The decorative brilliance was always doing serious work: it made the disquieting content beautiful enough to look at.

nodes.name: Vienna Secession
nodes.tagline: To every age its art, to art its freedom
nodes.summary: In 1897 a group of artists walked out of Vienna's conservative artists' association and built their own exhibition hall with that motto over the door. The Secession made room for art nouveau, symbolism and modern design in a city whose official taste was still historicist.

nodes.name: Congress of Vienna
nodes.tagline: Europe redrawn after Napoleon
nodes.summary: For nine months the powers that had defeated Napoleon met in Vienna to rebuild the map of Europe around a balance of power. The settlement was reactionary and it held: no general European war followed for ninety-nine years.

nodes.name: Wiener Schnitzel
nodes.tagline: A veal cutlet with a contested passport
nodes.summary: Pounded thin, breaded and fried until the coating puffs away from the meat, the schnitzel is Vienna's most exported object. A persistent story has it arriving from Milan with Field Marshal Radetzky, which food historians have never been able to substantiate.

nodes.name: Habsburg Monarchy
nodes.tagline: The dynasty that married its way across Europe
nodes.summary: From a minor Swiss castle the Habsburgs accumulated crowns for six hundred years, largely by arranging marriages rather than winning battles. The multi-ethnic empire they assembled dissolved in 1918, leaving behind a dozen nation states and one very large bureaucracy.

nodes.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
nodes.tagline: Twice decided he had finished philosophy
nodes.summary: Heir to one of Vienna's great fortunes, Wittgenstein gave the money away and wrote a book he believed had solved every philosophical problem, then returned twenty years later to dismantle it. Both the early and the late work turn on the same suspicion: that language quietly sets the limits of thought.

nodes.summary: Self-taught and stubborn, Schoenberg followed late-Romantic chromaticism until tonality gave out, then spent a decade devising the twelve-tone method to organise what was left. He insisted he had not destroyed tradition but continued it by the only honest route available.

nodes.summary: Freud argued that dreams are disguised wish fulfilments, and that the disguise follows rules — condensation, displacement, symbolism — which can be read backwards. It sold six hundred copies in eight years and then changed the century.

nodes.name: Psychoanalysis
nodes.tagline: Treatment by talking, on the theory that the patient does not know what they mean
nodes.summary: Psychoanalysis holds that symptoms carry meaning, that the meaning is hidden from the person carrying it, and that a long conversation under particular rules can recover it. Its scientific status has been contested for a century; its cultural penetration has not.

nodes.name: Entropy
nodes.tagline: The reason the past is different from the future
nodes.summary: Entropy counts how many microscopic arrangements would look the same from outside, and it tends to increase simply because disordered arrangements vastly outnumber ordered ones. It is the only fundamental quantity in physics that distinguishes forwards from backwards in time.

nodes.name: Geometry
nodes.tagline: Earth-measuring, which stopped being about the Earth
nodes.summary: Geometry began as practical surveying in Egypt and Mesopotamia and became, in Greek hands, the first body of knowledge derived entirely by proof from stated assumptions. When the fifth postulate was finally dropped in the 1800s, entirely consistent non-Euclidean geometries appeared — one of which turned out to describe real space.

nodes.name: Claudius Ptolemy
nodes.tagline: Wrong about the centre, right about almost everything else
nodes.summary: Ptolemy built a geometric model that predicted planetary positions accurately enough to remain in use for fourteen centuries, at the cost of putting the Earth at the centre and adding epicycles to make it work. He also produced the standard atlas of the ancient world, with coordinates.

facts.label: Accuracy
facts.value: Good enough to use for 1,400 years

facts.label: Also wrote
facts.value: The Geography, with latitude and longitude

nodes.name: Almagest
nodes.tagline: Kept by its Arabic nickname, 'the greatest'
nodes.summary: Ptolemy's astronomical treatise contains a star catalogue, a model for each planet and the mathematics to predict where anything will be. Europe knew it for centuries only through Arabic translations, which is why it goes by an Arabic name.

edges.relation: Its Arabic transmission followed the routes

nodes.name: Alexander the Great
nodes.tagline: Never lost a battle, died at thirty-two
nodes.summary: In thirteen years Alexander took an empire stretching from Greece to the Punjab, founding cities as he went and spreading Greek language and thought across the ancient world. He left no succession plan, and his generals spent forty years dismantling what he built.

nodes.name: The Nile
nodes.tagline: A river that made a civilisation by flooding on schedule
nodes.summary: The Nile's annual flood deposited fertile silt with enough regularity that Egyptian agriculture, taxation, surveying and calendar all organised themselves around it. Predicting the flood was a state function, and re-measuring the fields afterwards is one origin of geometry.

facts.label: Annual flood
facts.value: Ended in 1970, with the Aswan High Dam

facts.label: Herodotus
facts.value: Egypt is the gift of the Nile

edges.inverse: Partly born from re-measuring its fields

nodes.name: Ancient Egypt
nodes.tagline: Three thousand years of continuity, then a very long silence
nodes.summary: Egyptian civilisation persisted with recognisable institutions, religion and script for longer than the span between its end and today. When the script finally fell out of use in the fourth century AD, the ability to read it vanished for fourteen hundred years.

nodes.name: Rosetta Stone
nodes.tagline: A tax decree that unlocked a civilisation
nodes.summary: A fragment of a fairly routine priestly decree, inscribed in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek — and because scholars could read the Greek, it gave them a parallel text. French soldiers found it in a wall; the British took it two years later.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: July 1799, at Rashid, by French soldiers

nodes.name: Jean-François Champollion
nodes.tagline: Taught himself Coptic to read a language nobody spoke
nodes.summary: Champollion realised that hieroglyphs were neither purely pictorial nor purely alphabetic but both at once, and that Coptic — still used liturgically — preserved the underlying language. He announced the breakthrough in 1822 and reportedly fainted afterwards.

facts.label: Key insight
facts.value: The script is phonetic and ideographic together

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: Fluent in Coptic, the language's late descendant

nodes.name: Hieroglyphs
nodes.tagline: Pictures that are also sounds, and sometimes both at once
nodes.summary: Egyptian hieroglyphic writing mixes signs standing for sounds, signs standing for things, and signs that silently specify which meaning is intended. Europe assumed for centuries that the pictures were mystical symbols, which is precisely why nobody could read them.

facts.label: Read
facts.value: In whichever direction the figures face

nodes.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
nodes.tagline: Rearranged Europe twice and lost it twice
nodes.summary: An artillery officer who became emperor, Napoleon reformed law, administration and education across the continent while fighting almost continuously for fifteen years. His invasion of Russia destroyed his army, and the peace made after his fall was designed specifically to prevent anyone like him again.

nodes.name: French Campaign in Egypt
nodes.tagline: A military failure that founded a discipline
nodes.summary: Napoleon took 167 scholars along with his army, and while the fleet was destroyed and the campaign collapsed, the scientists catalogued Egypt in twenty-three volumes. The expedition lost the war and started Egyptology.

nodes.name: Lighthouse of Alexandria
nodes.tagline: Stood for 1,600 years, then three earthquakes
nodes.summary: Built on the island of Pharos, the lighthouse was among the tallest structures in the world and gave several languages their word for lighthouse. Earthquakes brought it down in stages; its blocks were reused in a fort that still stands on the site.

nodes.name: Eratosthenes
nodes.tagline: Measured the planet with a stick and a shadow
nodes.summary: Told that the sun cast no shadow in a well at Syene at noon on the solstice, while it clearly did in Alexandria, Eratosthenes measured that angle and worked out the Earth's circumference to within a few percent. He was also chief librarian at Alexandria, and invented a still-used method for finding primes.

facts.label: Also invented
facts.value: The sieve for finding prime numbers

nodes.name: Circumference of the Earth
nodes.tagline: Known to within a few percent, 2,200 years ago
nodes.summary: Eratosthenes assumed the Earth was a sphere and the sun's rays parallel, measured a shadow angle of about 7.2 degrees, and scaled up by the distance between two Egyptian cities. Ptolemy later adopted a smaller figure, and that error is part of why Columbus thought Asia was reachable.

facts.label: Error
facts.value: Somewhere between 1% and 16%, depending on the stadion
